extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, instructors, and others interested in proof comprehension and presentation
extracted.subtask_description: A publications page listing PCRG members' papers related to proof evaluation, proof comprehension, and proof presentation; serves as a literature/resource list rather than an explicit rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Research into how proofs are evaluated by mathematicians and instructors, including what counts as a proof, admissibility of graphical inferences, disagreement among mathematicians, role of sourcing and authority, how points are assigned to student proofs, and interpretations of written comments on graded proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative works listed: Weber & Mejía Ramos (2019) on graphical inferences; Weber & Czocher (2019) on disagreement about what constitutes a proof; Weber (2018) on sourcing; Miller, Infante & Weber (2018) on assigning points; Byrne et al. (2018) on student interpretations of written comments; Dawkins & Weber (2017) on values and norms; Weber (2008) on how mathematicians determine if an argument is a valid proof; Inglis & Mejia-Ramos (2009) and related papers on authority and visual arguments. This section collects empirical studies and discussions that characterize standards and practices used when judging proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies and assessments focused on understanding how students and teachers comprehend proofs, including development and validation of proof-comprehension tests, students' epistemological frames, instructional interventions, and proofreading strategies to foster comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative works listed: Wasserman et al. (2018) on teachers' views; Krupnik, Weber & Fukawa-Connelly (2018) on students' epistemological frames; Mejía-Ramos et al. (2017) on developing/validating proof comprehension tests; Weber (2015) on proofreading strategies; Samkoff & Weber (2015) on instructional intervention outcomes; Mejia-Ramos & Weber (2014) and Weber & Mejia-Ramos (2011, 2014) on how mathematicians read proofs. This section groups empirical and methodological research about measuring and improving comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Work addressing how proofs should be presented pedagogically and communicatively: linguistic conventions, diagram usage in student proofs, lecture practices, features of a good pedagogical proof, and design of courses/lectures to improve understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative works listed: Mejía Ramos et al. (2019) on corpus linguistics for mathematical explanation; Lew & Mejía Ramos (2019) on linguistic conventions; Mejía Ramos & Weber (2019) on diagram usage in calculus proofs; Lai & Weber (2014, 2016) and Lai, Weber & Mejia-Ramos (2012) on features of good pedagogical proofs and pedagogical practice; Wasserman et al. (2019) and related papers on designing advanced mathematics courses and lecture comprehension. Use this section as a pointer to empirical and pedagogical recommendations concerning presentation and communication of proofs.
